n: This lecture is about phenacetin and salicylic acid. Plan: phenacetin and salicylic acid, acetylsalicylic acid, their toxicological significance and methods of analysis. Key terms: polar solvent, phenacetin and salicylic acid, acetylsalicylic acid. The topic is devoted to the analysis, in the isolate, of substances with weakly basic and acidic properties.

t: In which isolate these substances are examined
n: First let us establish in which isolate these substances are examined. The isolate obtained in an acid medium is examined for barbiturates, neutral substances, for example phenacetin, and organic acids, that is, salicylic and picric acids. In salicylic acid poisoning, it is isolated from the specimen with polar solvents in an acid medium. Phenacetin is isolated in an acid medium with acidified water or alcohol.

General description of phenacetin. Phenacetin is a white crystalline powder, sparingly soluble in water and readily soluble in organic solvents. It has antipyretic, analgesic and anti-cold action. In chemical structure it is benzene containing, in the para position, an ethoxy group, that is, C2H5O, and an acetylamino group, that is, NHCOCH3.

Names and identifiers of phenacetin. The Latin name is Phenacetinum, the international name Phenacetin, CAS number 62-44-2. The chemical name is N-(4-ethoxyphenyl)acetamide or 1-ethoxy-4-acetaminobenzene, that is, acetophenetidin. Synonyms: Acetophenetidin, Acetylphenetidin, Fenacetina, Paracetophenetidin and phenedin.

On the extraction of neutral substances. For neutral substances such as antifebrin and phenacetin, the effect of pH is small. They are well extracted by organic solvents in acid, neutral and alkaline media. Nevertheless, the acid isolate is examined for neutral substances, for example phenacetin. That is, the substance is isolated at any pH, while the examination is carried out in the acid isolate.

t: Phenacetin and salicylic acid: isolation conditions
n: We compare the isolation conditions of phenacetin and salicylic acid. Phenacetin is a neutral substance: the effect of pH is small, and it is well extracted in acid, neutral and alkaline media. Salicylic acid, as an organic acid, is isolated in an acid medium. Therefore the isolate obtained in an acid medium is examined for barbiturates, phenacetin and salicylic acid.

Physicochemical data of phenacetin. Chemical name N-(4-ethoxyphenyl)acetamide, neutral in nature, melting point 134-135 °C. Solubility: in chloroform 1:14, in ethanol 1:15, in ether 1:90, in water 1:1300. In appearance it is a white, odourless crystalline powder with a bitter taste.

The toxicological significance of phenacetin. Taken in a large dose, phenacetin can cause methaemoglobinaemia, anaemia and nephritis. When the preparation is not fully hydrolysed, the highly toxic n-phenetidine is formed. The hydrolysis product p-aminophenol is oxidised to form quinonimine, which acts on haemoglobin.

t: Hydrolysis of phenacetin and toxic products
n: Hydrolysis of phenacetin and toxic products. In the body, phenacetin is hydrolysed to form para-aminophenol. P-aminophenol is oxidised and converted to quinonimine. Quinonimine quickly oxidises and breaks down haemoglobin and itself returns to p-aminophenol. Thus the chain begins with phenacetin and ends with an action on haemoglobin.

Metabolism of phenacetin. As a result of dealkylation, paracetamol, n-phenetidine and n-aminophenol may be formed, and in hydrolysis 2-hydroxyphenacetin is formed. Part of the phenacetin is excreted in the urine as metabolites, and part as conjugates with glucuronide and sulphates. The half-life is 0.6-1.3 hours, and Vd is 1-2 L/kg.

Detecting phenacetin based on hydrolysis. Phenacetin is hydrolysed by heating with concentrated hydrochloric acid, then examined on the basis of the products formed. The reactions used are: formation of ethyl acetate, and the azo dye and indophenol formation reactions. Under the action of an alcoholic solution of alkali and chloroform, isonitrile is formed, the sign of which is an offensive smell.

The azo dye formation reaction. Because a primary aromatic amine is formed in hydrolysis, the azo dye reaction is used. 1-2 drops are evaporated and heated with 1 ml of concentrated HCl until the volume is halved. It is cooled, and 1 % NaNO2 and alkaline β-naphthol are added. If a red colour forms, this indicates phenacetin.

The chromic anhydride and nitrophenacetin reactions. 5-6 drops of the chloroform solution are dried, then boiled for 5 minutes with 1 ml of concentrated HCl. After cooling, 2 % chromic anhydride is added. A dark red colour forms from the oxidation of p-aminophenol. When heated with nitric acid, phenacetin forms yellow nitrophenacetin.

The reaction of phenacetin with nitric acid. When phenacetin is heated with a solution of nitric acid, yellow nitrophenacetin is formed. Remember: phenacetin is a white crystalline powder, sparingly soluble in water and readily soluble in organic solvents. Its amount is determined by the photocolorimetric method based on the azo dye formation reaction, that is, with the help of PEC or SP.

Additional qualitative reactions. With Liebermann's reagent, phenacetin forms a violet colour. Phenacetin forms characteristic microcrystals with the copper-iodine complex. In the preliminary examination of urine for phenacetin, the azo dye reaction is carried out on 1 ml of urine; a red colour should form.

We revise the qualitative reactions of phenacetin by table. When heated with nitric acid, phenacetin forms yellow nitrophenacetin. After hydrolysis, the azo dye reaction gives a red colour, the isonitrile reaction an offensive smell, and indophenol reactions are also used. An alcoholic solution of phenacetin gives a spectral maximum at 250 nm.

Examining phenacetin by thin-layer chromatography, that is, TLC. The plate is silica gel G with a layer thickness of 250 µm; a methanolic solution of HCl is sprayed on it. The mobile phase is a mixture of methanol and 25 % ammonia, in a ratio of 100:1.5. The detecting reagent is Dragendorff reagent. The Rf value is 0.38, and a brown spot forms.

Examining phenacetin by gas chromatography and HPLC. For GC, a glass column 2 m long with an internal diameter of 2 mm is taken, the phase is 3 % SE-30 Chromosorb G-HP, the carrier gas is nitrogen at 45 ml/min. The column temperature is raised slowly from 100 °C to 300 °C, retention index RI 1675. In HPLC the column is ODS Hypersil, 160 x 5 mm, 5 µm, UV detector 244 nm; the phenacetin peak emerges at 4.4 minutes.

The IR, mass and UV spectra of phenacetin. In the IR spectrum, in a KBr disc, absorption bands are observed at 1244, 1655, 1513, 1555, 1265 and 836 cm-1. In the mass spectrum there are peaks at 108, 109, 179, 137, 43, 81, 80 and 110 m/z. In the UV spectrum, an alcoholic solution of phenacetin gives a spectral maximum at 250 nm, and in 0.1 M hydrochloric acid solution the maximum is at 244 nm.

Quantitative analysis of phenacetin. Its amount is determined by the photocolorimetric method based on the azo dye formation reaction, that is, with the help of PEC or SP. Quantitative determination is also carried out by the spectrophotometric method from the UV spectrum. The GLC and HPLC methods are also indicated for quantitative determination.

Properties of salicylic acid. Salicylic acid forms fine needle-like, light, odourless crystals with a sour-sweet taste. It is poorly soluble in cold water, very soluble in hot water, and soluble in alcohol and ether; it melts at 159 °C. It distils with steam, so it can be isolated from a biological specimen by steam distillation.

The main figures for salicylic acid. It melts at 159 °C; it is poorly soluble in cold water and very soluble in hot water. 80 % of salicylates is excreted through the kidneys and is completely excreted within 24 hours, while 20 % is metabolised in the tissues. The sensitivity of the bromine water reaction is 1:40000. The UV maximum is 300 nm in 0.5 N NaOH and 302 nm in 0.1 N H2SO4.

The toxicological significance of salicylic acid. It has a toxic action on the body only in high doses; it is used in medicine, and drugs such as aspirin and salol are made from it. It was used for preserving food, but because of its toxic action the state abolished this. Therefore foodstuffs, too, are sometimes sent to the forensic chemistry laboratory as physical evidence.

Signs of salicylic acid poisoning. Headache, dizziness, ringing in the ears and weakening of hearing are observed. The patient has diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, and circulation and the rhythm of breathing are disturbed. Sometimes nervous changes occur and the phenomenon of collapse appears.

We compare the clinical picture of phenacetin and salicylate poisoning. Phenacetin in a large dose can cause methaemoglobinaemia, anaemia and nephritis. The reason is that in the body it is hydrolysed and forms quinonimine, which acts on haemoglobin. In salicylic acid poisoning, headache, ringing in the ears, weakened hearing, diarrhoea and collapse are observed.

Metabolism of salicylic acid. Salicylates are absorbed from the stomach into the blood extremely quickly and bind to proteins as the sodium salt. They are mainly, to the extent of 80 %, excreted through the kidneys; they appear quickly in the urine and are completely excreted within 24 hours. The remaining 20 % is metabolised in the tissues to form 2,3-dihydroxybenzoic, 2,5-dihydroxybenzoic and 2,3,5-trihydroxybenzoic acids.

t: Isolating salicylic acid from the specimen
n: Isolating salicylic acid from the specimen. In salicylic acid poisoning, it is isolated from the specimen with polar solvents in an acid medium. The second possibility: salicylic acid distils with steam, so it can be isolated from a biological specimen by steam distillation. Foodstuffs may also be sent to the forensic chemistry laboratory as physical evidence.

Conditions for detecting salicylic acid. In forensic chemical analysis, salicylic acid is determined at the instruction of the court officers. Or it is determined only when the residue left after evaporating the solution under examination is characteristic of this acid. Some people can be quickly poisoned by salicylic acid. Accidents have also occurred when methyl ester was drunk instead of an alcoholic drink.

The reaction with iron(III) chloride. Salicylic acid forms a blue-violet colour with iron(III) chloride. The composition and colour of the complex depend on the pH of the reaction medium: monosalicylate, disalicylate and trisalicylate may be formed. According to the table, at pH 1.8-2.5 it is bluish-pink, at 4-8 red-brown, at 8-11 yellow. The colour formed does not disappear under the action of alcohol, which is the difference from phenol.

t: Limitations of the iron(III) chloride reaction
n: Limitations of the iron(III) chloride reaction. The reaction is characteristic when there are no substances that bind the phenolic hydroxyl, such as maltol and others. The colour does not disappear under the action of alcohol; that is the difference from phenol. Because the composition of the complex depends on pH, the pH must be controlled. As a result the Fe(III)-salicylate complex is formed, and its colour is blue-violet.

The reaction with bromine water. Bromine water, when salicylic acid is present in the solution, forms a white precipitate, that is, tribromophenol, and CO2 is released. The reaction is not characteristic of salicylic acid, because many organic substances containing a benzene ring give the same result. The sensitivity is 1:40000. If no reaction occurs, there is no salicylic acid or similar substance in the solution.

t: Significance of the salicylic acid reactions
n: The significance of the salicylic acid reactions. The iron(III) chloride reaction is characteristic: the colour does not disappear under the action of alcohol, which is the difference from phenol, when there are no substances binding the phenolic hydroxyl. The bromine water reaction is not characteristic but is very sensitive; if it does not occur, there is no salicylic acid, that is, it has negative significance. The smell of methyl salicylate and the UV maxima, 300 and 302 nm, are confirmatory signs.

t: Methyl salicylate and the UV spectrum
n: Methyl salicylate and the UV spectrum. If salicylic acid is heated with methyl alcohol in a concentrated sulphuric acid medium, the smell of the methyl ester of salicylic acid is noticed. Ethyl alcohol may also be used instead of methyl alcohol. In the UV spectrum, a solution in 0.5 N sodium hydroxide absorbs light maximally at 300 nm, and a solution in 0.1 N sulphuric acid at 302 nm.

t: Bromine water reaction: the logic of negative significance
n: The logic of the negative significance of the bromine water reaction. Bromine water in a solution of salicylic acid forms a white precipitate, that is, tribromophenol, and CO2 is released. The reaction is not characteristic: many organic substances containing a benzene ring give the same. Therefore, if no reaction occurs, the conclusion is drawn that there is no salicylic acid or similar substance in the solution under examination.

t: Preliminary examination of blood and urine
n: Preliminary examination of blood and urine. If Trinder's reagent, that is, a mixture of HgCl2 and Fe(NO3)3, is added to blood serum or urine, a red-crimson colour forms when salicylic acid is present. If a solution of iron(III) nitrate in nitric acid is added dropwise to urine or blood serum, a red-crimson colour also forms. These two reactions are recommended for preliminary examination.

Quantitative determination of salicylic acid. Making use of its acidic property, it is titrated with alkali. The bromatometric, that is, volumetric, method is also used. A solution in alkali or sulphuric acid is determined by UV spectrophotometry.

Relation to aspirin and paracetamol. Salicylic acid is used in the pharmaceutical industry to make drugs such as aspirin and salol. The toxic action of salicylic acid and its derivatives has been taken into account; to determine them, foodstuffs are sometimes also sent. Paracetamol is one of the metabolites formed in the dealkylation of phenacetin.

Let us summarise. Phenacetin is a neutral substance: it is determined by the azo dye reaction after hydrolysis, red colour, by the CrO3 reaction, dark red colour, by nitration, yellow colour, and by the UV maximum at 250 nm. Salicylic acid: a pH-dependent colour with FeCl3, a white precipitate with bromine water, the smell of methyl salicylate, and UV at 300 and 302 nm. 80 % of salicylates is excreted through the kidneys, and the remaining 20 % is metabolised in the tissues. For self-check: explain the pH dependence of the FeCl3 complex and the negative significance of the bromine water reaction.
